title: Do You Know Who I Am
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article uses golfer Scottie Scheffler's 2024 arrest outside the PGA Championship as a case study in humility under pressure, noting he complied fully with police instructions and didn't reveal his identity or status until well into the booking process. The author's central point is what Scheffler didn't say -- he never invoked his fame to demand different treatment, the classic 'Do you know who I am?' impulse the piece explicitly criticizes. This restraint is framed as a broader leadership lesson: making a chaotic situation about your own importance nearly always makes it worse, while making yourself deliberately unimportant can de-escalate it. The piece closes noting Scheffler still made his tee time and played well, reinforcing his composure under pressure.
points: Golfer Scottie Scheffler's compliant, low-drama behavior during a 2024 arrest is used as a leadership case study.
Scheffler never invoked his fame or status to demand different treatment -- he simply complied.
The article criticizes the 'Do you know who I am?' impulse as self-important behavior that worsens chaotic situations.
Making yourself deliberately unimportant in a tense moment is framed as a genuine leadership skill.
quotes: By now, anyone with an internet connection knows that the top-ranked golfer in the world, Scottie Scheffler, was arrested while driving to the golf course at the PGA Championship in Kentucky.
Scheffler didn’t make it about himself, his status, or his fame.
Most impressively, he never uttered the words, “Do you know who I am?” Those are ugly words to anyone who understands leadership.
Taking situations more seriously than themselves is what good people and leaders do.
In Scheffler’s case, the only way to de-escalate the conflict was to make himself unimportant in the moment.
Taking oneself too seriously is a challenge many leaders face and fail.
